title: Gadgets in everyday life: seven short texts
texts: A single slim device, not much heavier than a postcard, can hold a thousand novels. The text can be enlarged for tired eyes, and a built-in dictionary explains difficult words with one touch. Holidaymakers no longer need to sacrifice a pair of shoes to make room for books in a suitcase. Fans of paper still insist that nothing replaces the smell of a new page, but the argument is mostly about habit.

The small screen strapped to the arm now does much more than show the time. It counts every step, measures the heartbeat during a run, and gently vibrates when its owner has been sitting for an hour. Many users say it works like a personal trainer who never loses patience, although it cannot do the exercise for them. Some wearers, however, become obsessed with numbers and feel guilty about a quiet day.

Two people who share no common language can now hold a conversation: each wears a tiny earphone, and the device renders the other person's sentences almost instantly. The results are not flawless, and jokes tend to lose their sparkle on the way, but for ordering a meal or asking the way they work remarkably well. The technology has become so cheap that language schools are starting to wonder about their future.

Every helpful device is also a small witness. Speakers wait for a keyword and so keep their microphones switched on, watches record where we go and how well we sleep, and companies store this data for purposes that are not always clear. Experts advise reading the settings carefully and switching off what you do not need, though few of us have the patience to do so before the first use.

A flat disc the size of a large plate moves quietly around the whole house while the family is out, finds its way round chairs and returns to its base when the battery runs low. Owners claim that the floors are cleaner than before, although the machine sometimes gets stuck under the sofa or swallows a sock. People who once spent their Saturdays with a mop find themselves with an extra afternoon.

Place a small speaker on a shelf, and the room begins to obey. Spoken commands switch on music from an endless library, set a timer for the pasta, read the weather forecast or dim the lamps. Grandparents, who dislike buttons, are often its biggest fans, and children use it as a patient language coach. The only drawback is the confusion when guests hear a voice reply from nowhere.

Sooner or later, most of us find ourselves in a café, scanning the walls for a free socket. A device that stores spare power and fits into a coat pocket solves the problem, which is why such little blocks have become as common as keys. Experts are not sure whether the real cause of the worry is the poor endurance of telephones or our own refusal to be out of contact even for an hour.
